definition: One 1U drawer of an NVL72 rack holding two superchip boards (2 CPUs + 4 GPUs), their network cards, local SSDs and cold plates. Eighteen compute trays make up the rack's 72 GPUs.
A 1U drawer of power supplies that converts the building's AC power into low-voltage DC for a rack; in a GB200 NVL72 each shelf holds six 5.5 kW supplies (up to 33 kW).
A thick copper bar running the height of a rack that carries DC power from the power shelves to every tray. At ~50 V a 132 kW rack draws about 2,600 A, which is why higher voltages are coming.

Cooling in which liquid flows through cold plates mounted on the hottest chips (GPUs, CPUs, switches), removing most of the heat at the source; the remaining heat is handled by fans or a rear-door exchanger.
Cooling in which whole servers sit in a tank of non-conductive fluid (single-phase) or a fluid that boils on the chips (two-phase). Very dense, but it changes how hardware is serviced and qualified.
A transitional setup in which a rack's coolant loop dumps its heat into room air through a sidecar radiator, so liquid-cooled racks can run in halls without facility water.

Heat leaving a surface per unit area, here watts per square centimetre of chip. Higher flux needs a coolant that carries more heat per unit volume: water holds roughly 3,500 times more heat per litre than air.
An AI-factory output metric: how many tokens a fleet generates each second for every megawatt of power it draws, at a stated speed per user. It turns a fixed power budget into revenue capacity.
How fast each user receives generated tokens. Serving more users at once raises tokens per GPU but lowers interactivity, so throughput figures are only comparable at the same interactivity.
NVIDIA's operations software for AI factories (2025): provisions and monitors DGX racks, diagnoses failures and schedules jobs by combining Base Command Manager with Run:ai.

The line of projects waiting for a grid operator to study and approve a connection to the transmission network. In the US the median wait from request to operation for new generation exceeds four years.
How long it takes a datacenter site to obtain the electricity it needs, from utility request to energized capacity. For AI builds it is often longer than constructing the building.

Power plants (often gas turbines, engines or fuel cells) built on or next to a datacenter site and feeding it directly rather than through the utility grid, used to start before a grid connection arrives.
Running new hardware at full load for days before accepting it into production, to flush out early failures in GPUs, cables, cooling and power before customers rely on them.
A GPU's share of everything a datacenter must provision to run it: the GPU, its host CPU, switches and NICs, plus cooling and conversion losses. Per-MW metrics divide by this, not by GPU TDP.
